power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 3 codebook/README/label sources and 393 data columns across 28 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (10 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``figure``, ``file_stem``, ``panel`, `row`, `col`` while the data has `figure`, `file_stem`, `panel`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 28 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

This module also assesses whether the paper's Python code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 14 Python code files.
#### Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no `source()`-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an `import` loads a module, not the paper's own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

**5 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `leistung_natural.csv` to `results/06_report/leistung_natural.csv` (in ensembles.py); `mi_ensemble_natural.csv` to `results/06_report/mi_ensemble_natural.csv` (in evaluation.py); `leistung_natural.csv` to `results/06_report/leistung_natural.csv` (in evaluation.py); `auprc_natural.csv` to `results/06_report/auprc_natural.csv` (in evaluation.py); `kalibrierung_kennzahlen.csv` to `results/06_report/kalibrierung_kennzahlen.csv` (in evaluation.py). #### Execution

**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 14 scripts: 6 ran without error, 4 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 3 files were not run on their own, because other files import them: common.py (by checks.py, evaluation.py, mc_dropout.py, training.py, run_pipeline.py, uncertainty.py); feature_mapping.py (by mimic_dataset.py, prepare_eicu.py); architectures.py (by checks.py, common.py, evaluation.py, mc_dropout.py, training.py, run_pipeline.py, uncertainty.py). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`).

text.text: Clinical prediction models often perform worse after transfer between hospital systems, but deterioration becomes apparent only once outcomes are known.
We investigated whether uncertainty measures available at prediction time warn of performance loss and can help identify individual predictions requiring review.
Three neural network architectures were trained on MIMIC-IV for in-hospital mortality prediction and evaluated on eICU-CRD.
Measures included predictive entropy, mutual information from Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensembles, and representation density.
After transfer, AUROC fell from 0.86-0.87 to 0.76-0.77 and calibration worsened, while entropy and mutual information were lower.
None of the measures reliably indicated the reduced performance.

Deferring the 20% with the highest entropy reduced the remaining error rate from 17.5-20.1% to 6.3-8.0%; the deferred patients included 91-99% of false alarms but only 2-7% of missed deaths, which carried low uncertainty.
Uncertainty therefore supported selective review but failed to reveal performance loss.
Clinical prediction models, based on multimodal data, are increasingly deployed to detect deterioration and personalize treatment decisions [1] [2] [3] .
text.formatted: Clinical prediction models, based on multimodal data, are increasingly deployed to detect deterioration and personalize treatment decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> .

text.text: Sequential deep learning models, including recurrent neural networks and transformers, have shown strong performance in intensive care time-series prediction 4, 5 .
text.formatted: Sequential deep learning models, including recurrent neural networks and transformers, have shown strong performance in intensive care time-series prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> .

text.text: However, very few medical providers can train their own models tailored to their patient population and medical practice.
Increasingly, providers will deploy prediction models locally that are trained elsewhere.
It is well-known that models developed using data from a single institution or health system may not generalize to other settings, and external validation remains uncommon 4 .
text.formatted: It is well-known that models developed using data from a single institution or health system may not generalize to other settings, and external validation remains uncommon <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: Differences in patient populations, clinical practice, and measurement processes can compromise discrimination and calibration when models are transferred between institutions 5, 6 .
text.formatted: Differences in patient populations, clinical practice, and measurement processes can compromise discrimination and calibration when models are transferred between institutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: This deterioration may not be adequately reflected in model confidence 7, 8.
text.formatted: This deterioration may not be adequately reflected in model confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref>.

text.text: Consider a mortality prediction model trained in one hospital and used in another: it may return an estimate of 4% for a certain patient whose actual risk is several times higher.
Nothing in the output signals that this estimate deserves less trust than one at the development site.
Such failures can go unnoticed in routine care.
A widely implemented proprietary sepsis model reached an AUROC of 0.63 in independent external validation, compared with 0.76 to 0.83 reported by its developer.
It missed two thirds of patients with sepsis while alerting on 18% of all inpatients, and the shortfall was detected only retrospectively, from outcomes, after the model had entered routine use 9.
text.formatted: It missed two thirds of patients with sepsis while alerting on 18% of all inpatients, and the shortfall was detected only retrospectively, from outcomes, after the model had entered routine use <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref>.

text.text: Explainable AI (XAI) is a widely studied approach helping clinicians judge whether a prediction can be relied on 10 , yet clinical XAI evaluations rarely test whether explanations help clinicians detect incorrect predictions 11 .
text.formatted: Explainable AI (XAI) is a widely studied approach helping clinicians judge whether a prediction can be relied on <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> , yet clinical XAI evaluations rarely test whether explanations help clinicians detect incorrect predictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: Explanations aim to show which inputs drove a prediction, not whether it is likely to be correct, and they can appear plausible for incorrect outputs 12 .
text.formatted: Explanations aim to show which inputs drove a prediction, not whether it is likely to be correct, and they can appear plausible for incorrect outputs <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Uncertainty quantification offers an alternative approach: it communicates alongside each prediction how cautiously the risk estimate should be treated 13 and may flag unfamiliar inputs, potentially incorrect predictions, or cases that warrant human review 14, 15 .
text.formatted: Uncertainty quantification offers an alternative approach: it communicates alongside each prediction how cautiously the risk estimate should be treated <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> and may flag unfamiliar inputs, potentially incorrect predictions, or cases that warrant human review <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: Such measures may matter most where clinicians' own error detection is weakest.

Whether a given uncertainty measure actually flags incorrect predictions, however, has to be established with labeled data, as for calibration, and may depend on the data and the type of distribution shift.

For in-hospital mortality prediction, evaluation of discrimination and calibration requires outcomes that become available only after predictions have been made, introducing a significant time lag between deployment and model validation.
Uncertainty measures, by contrast, can be computed at the time of prediction, before the outcome is known 14 .
text.formatted: Uncertainty measures, by contrast, can be computed at the time of prediction, before the outcome is known <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: By identifying outputs that require closer scrutiny, uncertainty quantification may complement model interpretation and support human oversight.

It may also complement outcome-based evaluation within post-market monitoring frameworks for high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act and for medical devices under the Medical Device Regulation 16, 17.
text.formatted: It may also complement outcome-based evaluation within post-market monitoring frameworks for high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act and for medical devices under the Medical Device Regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref>.

text.text: While our framework applies to all prediction tasks based on clinical routine data, we focus on in-hospital mortality as an example.

Loss of performance after transfer has been reported across clinical prediction tasks 18 , and mortality prediction is no exception: ICU models developed at one institution lose discrimination and calibration at others 4, 5 , as do established severity scores such as APACHE and SAPS, which require recalibration outside their development populations 19.
text.formatted: Loss of performance after transfer has been reported across clinical prediction tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> , and mortality prediction is no exception: ICU models developed at one institution lose discrimination and calibration at others <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> , as do established severity scores such as APACHE and SAPS, which require recalibration outside their development populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref>.

text.text: In this article, we consider uncertainty measures that may indicate performance deterioration before outcome labels are available and we evaluate them for three evaluation levels.

Cohort separation asks whether a measure distinguishes external from development cohort patients; error detection asks whether it ranks incorrect above correct predictions within the target cohort, and selective prediction asks whether deferring high uncertainty cases -withholding the model's prediction and referring the patient to clinical review -reduces error among retained predictions.

Previous medical-AI studies have examined these objectives in different settings, including out-of-distribution detection in clinical tabular data 20 , failure detection in medical imaging 21 , and selective prediction in multimodal intensive care data 22 .
text.formatted: Previous medical-AI studies have examined these objectives in different settings, including out-of-distribution detection in clinical tabular data <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> , failure detection in medical imaging <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> , and selective prediction in multimodal intensive care data <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> .

text.text: In ICU mortality prediction, uncertainty methods have been evaluated on artificially altered patient records from MIMIC-III 23 and for sepsis prediction across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD and HiRID, strategies for adapting deep learning models to a new site have been compared systematically 24.
text.formatted: In ICU mortality prediction, uncertainty methods have been evaluated on artificially altered patient records from MIMIC-III <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> and for sepsis prediction across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD and HiRID, strategies for adapting deep learning models to a new site have been compared systematically <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, uncertainty estimates can deteriorate under dataset shift 7 , and on medical tabular data neither uncertainty estimates 25 nor dedicated out-of-distribution detectors 20 have reliably identified patients from a shifted population.
text.formatted: Moreover, uncertainty estimates can deteriorate under dataset shift <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> , and on medical tabular data neither uncertainty estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> nor dedicated out-of-distribution detectors <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> have reliably identified patients from a shifted population.

text.text: Specifically, we evaluate output-, sampling-, and representation-based uncertainty measures for in-hospital mortality prediction under transfer from MIMIC-IV to eICU-CRD.

After quantifying changes in discrimination and calibration, we assess each measure for (1) cohort separation, (2) prediction-error detection in the external cohort, and (3) selective prediction through uncertainty-based deferral.
We investigate the following research questions: 1) Do uncertainty measures increase after transfer to another hospital system, as a warning of deteriorating performance would require?
2) Do uncertainty measures identify the individual predictions that are likely to be wrong?
3) When human resources allow for manual review of a limited share of predictions, can the above measures suggest which patients to review to lower error rates?
The first question asks whether a measure registers that the patient population has changed; the second and third ask whether it registers that an individual prediction is unreliable.
These are different properties, and a measure can have one without the other.
Each question corresponds to one evaluation level described in the Methods: cohort separation, error detection, and selective prediction.
We report three base architectures (LSTM, GRU and transformer); each trained with ten random seeds.
Values are means over the ten seed models; brackets give the 95% t-interval over seeds.
Where two cohorts are compared, the difference was computed within each seed before averaging, so that the interval describes the paired difference across training runs.
The internal test set comprised 7,298 ICU stays from MIMIC-IV with an in-hospital mortality of 13.8%, and the external cohort 66,934 stays from eICU-CRD with a mortality of 10.9% (Table 1; Table 2).
text.formatted: The internal test set comprised 7,298 ICU stays from MIMIC-IV with an in-hospital mortality of 13.8%, and the external cohort 66,934 stays from eICU-CRD with a mortality of 10.9% (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>; Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: The external cohort was similar to the internal test set in age (median 66 vs 67 years) and sex (45.9% vs 44.6% women) but had a lower in-hospital mortality (10.9% vs 13.8%).

Of 94,458 ICU stays in MIMIC-IV, we excluded 16,911 stays from admissions with more than one ICU stay and 40,899 stays shorter than 48 hours, leaving 36,648 stays from 31,459 patients; MIMIC-IV contains adults only.
The training pool comprised 29,350 stays from 25,168 patients and the internal test set 7,298 stays from 6,291 patients, with in-hospital mortality of 12.9% and 13.8% (Table 1).
text.formatted: The training pool comprised 29,350 stays from 25,168 patients and the internal test set 7,298 stays from 6,291 patients, with in-hospital mortality of 12.9% and 13.8% (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: In eICU-CRD, 1,751 of 200,859 ICU stays were first excluded because no hospital discharge status was recorded, so that no outcome can be derived.

A further 618 stays were excluded for age below 18 years, 121,537 for an ICU stay shorter than 48 hours, and 10,019 for belonging to an admission with more than one ICU stay, leaving 66,934 stays with in-hospital mortality of 10.9% (Table 2).
text.formatted: A further 618 stays were excluded for age below 18 years, 121,537 for an ICU stay shorter than 48 hours, and 10,019 for belonging to an admission with more than one ICU stay, leaving 66,934 stays with in-hospital mortality of 10.9% (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: The single-stay criterion was applied at a different point in the two databases.

In MIMIC-IV, ICU stays per admission were counted in the raw data, so that an admission with one short and one long ICU stay was excluded entirely; in eICU-CRD, they were counted after the other criteria, so that the long stay of such an admission was retained.
As a result, 10,378 external stays (15.5%) belong to admissions that the MIMIC-IV rule would have excluded.
Restricting the external cohort to the remaining 56,556 stays changed no finding (Supplementary Table 2).
text.formatted: Restricting the external cohort to the remaining 56,556 stays changed no finding (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Table 1 | MIMIC-IV v3.1, development and internal test cohorts Step ICU stays (patients) ICU stays in the database 94,458 Admission with more than one ICU stay, counted in the raw data -16,911 → 77,547 Age below 18 years -0 → 77,547 ICU stay shorter than 48 h -40,899 → 36,648 Eligible stays 36,648 (31,459) Training pool, 80% of patients 29,350 (25,168) -model training 23,472 -validation: hyperparameter selection 5,878 Internal test set, 20% of patients 7,298 (6,291) In-hospital mortality, training pool / test 12.9% / 13.8% Table 2 | eICU-CRD v2.0, external transfer cohort Step ICU stays ICU stays in the database 200,859 Without a recorded hospital discharge status -1,751 → 199,108 Age below 18 years -618 →198,490 ICU stay shorter than 48 h -121,537 → 76,953 Admission with more than one ICU stay, counted after the filters above -10,019 → 66,934 External transfer cohort 66,934 In-hospital mortality 10.9% No training or validation; all included stays were used for evaluation only.
Discrimination declined in all models after transfer.
On the internal test set, the AUROC was between 0.858 and 0.873; after transfer it fell to 0.762-0.773, a loss close to 0.10 in every architecture, with seed intervals that excluded zero (Table 3).
text.formatted: On the internal test set, the AUROC was between 0.858 and 0.873; after transfer it fell to 0.762-0.773, a loss close to 0.10 in every architecture, with seed intervals that excluded zero (Table <ref type="table">3</ref>).

text.text: On the precision-recall scale, the AUPRC fell from 3.7 to 4.2 times the mortality rate to 3.1 to 3.5 times.
Deep ensembles of the ten seed models raised the AUROC by 0.004 to 0.009 but lost as much after transfer as single models.
The predicted risks also became too extreme after transfer: patients given a high risk died less often than predicted, and patients given a low risk died more often.

This is measured by the calibration slope, which is 1 for a well-calibrated model and below 1 when predicted risks are more extreme than observed risks; it fell from 0.84 to 0.96 in-domain to 0.57 to 0.64 after transfer (Table 3, Fig. 1).
text.formatted: This is measured by the calibration slope, which is 1 for a well-calibrated model and below 1 when predicted risks are more extreme than observed risks; it fell from 0.84 to 0.96 in-domain to 0.57 to 0.64 after transfer (Table <ref type="table">3</ref>, Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Deep ensembles were better calibrated in-domain, with slopes of 0.94 to 1.01, but fell to 0.60 to 0.67 after transfer.

The decline has the same origin as the loss of discrimination: the spread of the risk estimates within the outcome groups was unchanged, but survivors and non-survivors moved closer together, so that estimates of the same size were too extreme (Supplementary Note 5).
On average, the models underestimated mortality to a similar degree in both cohorts.
For every 100 deaths the GRU expected, 133 occurred in MIMIC-IV and 134 in eICU-CRD; for the LSTM, 119 and 119; for the transformer, 113 and 112.
The transfer therefore changed how extreme the individual risk estimates were, not their overall level.

text.text: Predictive entropy and mutual information did not rise after transfer; both were slightly lower for patients in the external hospital system, and only representation density and the logit variance were weakly higher.

For each uncertainty measure, we asked how often a randomly chosen external patient had a higher value than a randomly chosen internal patient, with 0.5 corresponding to chance (Supplementary Table 6).

text.text: The predictive entropy of the single models separated the cohorts at 0.475, 0.466, and 0.462 for the GRU, LSTM, and transformer, below chance in every architecture and every seed.

The mutual information, which measures how much the repeated predictions for the same patient vary, was also lower on the external cohort: 0.477, 0.476, and 0.464 for Monte Carlo dropout and 0.474, 0.488, and 0.457 for deep ensembles, respectively.
The total predictive uncertainty of both procedures separated the cohorts similarly weakly and in the same direction.
Mutual information accounted for 0.9% to 2.7% of the total predictive uncertainty in both cohorts (mean mutual information divided by mean total uncertainty).

Only two uncertainty measures were higher on the external cohort, and only weakly: the representation density, at 0.516, 0.531, and 0.512, with seed intervals above 0.5, and the logitvariance component of Monte Carlo dropout, at 0.527, 0.533, and 0.533 (Fig. 2, Supplementary Table 6, Supplementary Fig. 2).

The entropy of the single models identified errors with AUROCs of 0.856, 0.858, and 0.870 for the GRU, LSTM, and transformer.

Representation density and the logitvariance component, the only two uncertainty measures that had been slightly higher overall in the new hospital system, were less useful for spotting individual errors: the density identified errors less well than the entropy, and the logit variance tended to be higher for correct than for wrong predictions (Supplementary Table 6).

The epistemic components did less well.
Mutual information reached 0.810, 0.791, and 0.836 for Monte Carlo dropout and 0.780 to 0.855 for deep ensembles.

The representation density reached 0.789, 0.728, and 0.753; its paired difference to the predictive entropy ranged from -0.067 to -0.130 across all seven configurations and excluded zero in each (Supplementary Fig. 3).

text.text: The logit-variance component showed inverse behavior, at 0.181 to 0.326: patients whose predictions varied most between passes were more often correctly classified.
Deferring the most uncertain patients to clinical review left markedly fewer misclassifications among the remaining patients.

With the 20% most uncertain patients deferred by the predictive entropy of the single model, the misclassification rate among the remaining patients fell from 17.5%, 18.9%, and 20.1% to 6.3%, 6.7%, and 8.0% for the GRU, LSTM, and transformer; with the predictive entropy of the deep ensemble, it fell to 6.0%, 6.1%, and 8.0% (Fig. 3; Supplementary Fig. 6).

Deferring by mutual information (0.047 to 0.056), by representation density (0.048 to 0.072, 1.3 to 1.8 times the excess area of the entropy; Supplementary Fig. 4), or by the logit-variance component (0.273 to 0.365) was worse in every architecture.

text.text: On the internal test set the predictive entropy of the single model identified errors with AUROCs of 0.873, 0.878, and 0.878, that is 0.017, 0.020, and 0.007 higher than on the external cohort, and left an excess area under the risk-coverage curve of 0.026 to 0.028 against 0.037 to 0.042 after transfer (Supplementary Table 12).

text.text: The ranking of the measures was the same in both cohorts.
Taken together, higher uncertainty after transfer did not imply better performance in error detection or selective prediction.
Predictive entropy was lower in the external cohort but remained as the most useful measure for identifying errors and prioritizing predictions for review (Fig. 4).

text.text: At a classification threshold of 0.5, every uncertainty measure identified errors less well.

The Monte Carlo entropy and the single-model entropy stayed within 0.01 of each other at both thresholds (0.761 vs 0.755, 0.753 vs 0.744, and 0.770 vs 0.767 at 0.5), and the density on length-normalized representations exceeded the singlemodel entropy for the GRU (0.764 vs 0.755; Supplementary Table 8, Supplementary Note 2).

text.text: Finally, 66 of the 70 trained models had reached their lowest validation loss before the final epoch of the fixed training length, and assessing each base model at that epoch instead of the end of training changed no conclusion (Supplementary Note 10; Supplementary Table 10; Supplementary Table 11).

text.text: After transfer to another hospital system, discrimination and calibration declined, but no uncertainty measure rose to signal this loss: predictive entropy and mutual information were in fact lower in the external cohort.

Within the external cohort uncertainty however identified the single predictions most likely to be wrong, and deferring the most uncertain patients removed most misclassifications, mostly false alarms, from the predictions that remained.

The uncertainty measure that served best on both patient-level questions was the simplest one, the predictive entropy of the model itself; sampling-based and distance-based uncertainty measures added little or did worse.
Uncertainty, as measured by predictive entropy, thus ranked predictions by their reliability but did not reveal that the model as a whole had become less reliable.

Most external patients received a low predicted risk of death (Supplementary Fig. 1); predictions near 0% or 100% have low entropy, whereas predictions near 50% have high entropy because survival and death are considered equally likely.
text.formatted: Most external patients received a low predicted risk of death (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>); predictions near 0% or 100% have low entropy, whereas predictions near 50% have high entropy because survival and death are considered equally likely.

text.text: Low entropy therefore indicates a more certain prediction, not a correct one: it decreased even though the models became less able to distinguish survivors from non-survivors and produced overly extreme risk estimates (calibration slopes below 1).

Ovadia et al. 7 showed that good calibration on the original data does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimates when the data change; transfer between hospital systems is a clinical instance of this.
text.formatted: Ovadia et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> showed that good calibration on the original data does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimates when the data change; transfer between hospital systems is a clinical instance of this.

text.text: Monitoring for an increase in entropy would have failed to flag the observed deterioration.
Disagreement between repeated predictions did not indicate the deterioration either; two properties of mutual information may explain why.

It accounted for only a few percent of the total predictive uncertainty, and for the GRU and the transformer the difference between cohorts largely disappeared when patients were compared within deciles of predicted risk (Supplementary Note 9), so that it partly reflected the distribution of predicted risks.
In addition, ensemble members and dropout passes may have made similar errors after transfer; agreement among repeated predictions does not imply that they are correct.

These results follow from what the measures estimate: entropy and mutual information describe the predicted outcome and can therefore rank errors but need not rise when the inputs change, whereas representation density describes the inputs and can register a change in the population but says nothing about whether a given prediction is correct.

That the density separated the cohorts only weakly leaves two explanations: the two cohorts look alike in the learned representation, or the representation or the density estimator overlooked the changes that mattered for prediction.

The outcome is in line with Postels et al. 27 , who found that strong detection of unfamiliar inputs by deterministic methods does not guarantee reliable uncertainty under continuous distribution shift, and contrasts with the image-benchmark results of Mukhoti et al. 28 , where such densities matched deep ensembles.
text.formatted: The outcome is in line with Postels et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> , who found that strong detection of unfamiliar inputs by deterministic methods does not guarantee reliable uncertainty under continuous distribution shift, and contrasts with the image-benchmark results of Mukhoti et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> , where such densities matched deep ensembles.

text.text: Predictive entropy still helped identify patient-level errors within the external cohort.
Most correctly classified patients had very low predicted risks and low entropy.
Misclassified patients often had intermediate predicted risks, where entropy is higher.
When a fixed proportion of predictions is selected for review, what matters is whether incorrect predictions rank above correct ones.
Entropy can therefore help select individual predictions for review even when its overall level is lower in the external cohort.
Compared with the internal test set, error detection by entropy lost 0.007 to 0.020 in AUROC and the excess area rose by about a third.

After transfer, entropy still separated incorrect from correct predictions almost as well as at the development site, but it gave no indication that the model had moved to a hospital system where it performed worse.
Our main Gaussian density score identified errors best in the GRU, where it ranked patients most similarly to entropy.
The density based on length-normalized representations also followed entropy closely and performed best among the density measures (Supplementary Table 7).
text.formatted: The density based on length-normalized representations also followed entropy closely and performed best among the density measures (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">7</ref>).

text.text: High logit variance, which measures variation in the model's internal scores across dropout passes, tended to prioritize correct predictions for review (Supplementary Note 9).
High values often occurred at very low or very high predicted risks, where most classifications were correct.
At these extremes, substantial differences in internal scores can translate into only small differences in predicted probabilities.
This may partly explain why logit variance was a poor indicator of prediction errors.

The most actionable finding is that predictive entropy ranked errors within the external cohort and supported selective deferral: it requires no additional training or repeated passes, can be reported with every prediction 13 , and reviewing one in five patients would have reached about 70% of all misclassifications (Fig. 5; Supplementary Fig. 8).
text.formatted: The most actionable finding is that predictive entropy ranked errors within the external cohort and supported selective deferral: it requires no additional training or repeated passes, can be reported with every prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> , and reviewing one in five patients would have reached about 70% of all misclassifications (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref>; Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">8</ref>).

text.text: A prespecified entropy threshold, informed by the entropy on the internal test cohort, could trigger review of the patient record, missing measurements, and model output before the prediction informs care.

Whether entropy ranks errors in a new setting, and at which threshold, can itself only be verified once outcomes are known, as for calibration; in our transfer this property carried over with modest loss (Supplementary Table 12), but that is not guaranteed elsewhere.

text.text: Such a workflow could contribute to human oversight of high-risk AI systems under Article 14 of the EU AI Act 16 .
text.formatted: Such a workflow could contribute to human oversight of high-risk AI systems under Article 14 of the EU AI Act <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> .

text.text: The threshold should be chosen against an acceptable residual error rate and available review capacity and the rule must state which errors it targets: because entropy is highest at a predicted risk of 50% and low near 0%, the rule evaluated here selected almost exclusively false alarms, while most remaining errors were deaths among patients classified as low risk (Supplementary Table 9; Supplementary Fig. 8).

text.text: Such unflagged errors could create false reassurance, and low entropy should not waive critical review, especially when other clinical concerns are present.

How such information is presented matters: limited AI literacy has been identified as a barrier to using model transparency information for oversight 29 , which makes AI competencies an essential part of medical training 30 .

text.text: Post-market monitoring should not rely solely on the model's own uncertainty.
Article 72 of the EU AI Act and Article 83 of the Medical Device Regulation require ongoing monitoring of high-risk AI systems and medical devices, respectively 16, 17 .

text.text: Finlayson et al. 31 described how changes in patient populations, clinical practice, and data recording can undermine clinical AI systems.
text.formatted: Finlayson et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31</ref> described how changes in patient populations, clinical practice, and data recording can undermine clinical AI systems.

text.text: Our findings add that poorer performance need not be accompanied by increases in entropy or mutual information, but predictive entropy is a valuable uncertainty measure before true outcomes are known.
Monitoring should include regular checks of patient characteristics, missing measurements, and data recording practices, which can begin before outcomes are known.

Once outcomes become available, planned audits should assess how well the model still separates patients with and without the outcome of the event that the model predicts, how closely predicted risks match observed outcomes across the risk range, and how often clinically important errors occur.
These audits should specifically examine deaths among patients classified as low risk and check whether the review rule still selects the errors it was designed to identify.
Shared terminologies and standards-based repositories such as openEHR support data interoperability across institutions 32 .
text.formatted: Shared terminologies and standards-based repositories such as openEHR support data interoperability across institutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32</ref> .

text.text: However, harmonized data structures do not ensure model generalizability, making local validation and ongoing monitoring essential.
Although representation density separated the cohorts only weakly, tracking its distribution across many patients might help identify changes that warrant investigation.
Whether this provides a timely and reliable monitoring measure, including for changes within individual hospitals 33 , remains to be tested.
text.formatted: Whether this provides a timely and reliable monitoring measure, including for changes within individual hospitals <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33</ref> , remains to be tested.

text.text: As the models themselves gave no such clue, information on the model's development population may help clinicians assess whether it is being applied to patients and clinical settings similar to those in which it was developed 34.
text.formatted: As the models themselves gave no such clue, information on the model's development population may help clinicians assess whether it is being applied to patients and clinical settings similar to those in which it was developed <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34</ref>.

text.text: This study has three main limitations.

First, its scope: it examined a single prediction task, inhospital mortality from the first 48 hours, a single transfer between two US critical care databases, and 13 routinely charted variables, with glucose and pH as the only laboratory values and no medications.
The evaluation framework applies to other settings, but whether the findings, including the deferral results, hold for other outcomes, health systems, and richer inputs remains to be tested.
Second, the comparison of uncertainty methods is bounded in two ways.

Other distance-aware approaches, such as spectral-normalized Gaussian processes 35 and deterministic uncertainty quantification 36 , were not evaluated, and the encoder constraints bound distances only across the final layer, not end to end.
text.formatted: Other distance-aware approaches, such as spectral-normalized Gaussian processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> and deterministic uncertainty quantification <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36</ref> , were not evaluated, and the encoder constraints bound distances only across the final layer, not end to end.

text.text: Third, the design is retrospective and the statistics describe model variability, not patient sampling.

Intervals reflect variability across training runs on fixed cohorts; differences between the hospitals within eICU-CRD were not analyzed, and the breakdown of deferred errors was conducted after the main results were known.

Selective prediction was evaluated by deferring the most uncertain patients and measuring errors among the remaining ones; the consequences of false alarms and missed deaths were not weighed against each other, and how such deferral would affect clinical decisions in prospective use was not assessed.
After transfer between hospital systems, model discrimination and calibration worsened while predictive entropy decreased.

Representation density only weakly distinguished patients from the two cohorts, whereas predictive entropy was more useful for identifying errors and selecting predictions for review within the external cohort.
These findings highlight the distinction between detecting changes in the patient population and identifying individual prediction errors.
A model whose performance has worsened may nevertheless appear more confident.
Predictive entropy could help prioritize clinical review, but lower error rates among predictions not selected for review do not establish that review improves clinical decisions.
Under the review rule evaluated here, most remaining errors involved patients who died despite being classified as low risk.

Clinical use therefore requires validation in the receiving hospital and prospective evaluation of review thresholds and workflows, including which errors remain undetected and how much clinician time review requires.
Model performance should continue to be monitored after deployment as patient outcomes become available.
In this retrospective study we developed in-hospital mortality prediction models with MIMIC-IV v3.1 as the development database and eICU-CRD v2.0 as an external transfer cohort 37, 38 .
text.formatted: In this retrospective study we developed in-hospital mortality prediction models with MIMIC-IV v3.1 as the development database and eICU-CRD v2.0 as an external transfer cohort <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> .

text.text: Both are de-identified critical care databases from hospitals in the United States and are available through PhysioNet under credentialed access.
Both cohorts were restricted to adults, ICU stays of at least 48 hours, and hospital admissions with a single ICU stay; a patient with several hospital admissions contributes each of them.

MIMIC-IV patients were split at random, with 20% held out as the internal test set so that no patient contributes to both sets; the remaining 80% formed the training pool, part of which served as the validation split for hyperparameter selection.
All included eICU-CRD stays were used for evaluation only.
The outcome was in-hospital mortality, predicted from the first 48 hours of the ICU stay, following the benchmark task of Harutyunyan et al 39 .
text.formatted: The outcome was in-hospital mortality, predicted from the first 48 hours of the ICU stay, following the benchmark task of Harutyunyan et al <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39</ref> .

text.formatted: Thirteen routinely charted variables were extracted for each of the 48 hours (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Multiple measurements within one hour were averaged, as in MIMIC-Extract 40 rather than represented by the last measurement as in the logic of Harutyunyan et al.

The in-hospital mortality rate of the training pool was 12.88% (Table 1).

text.text: We compared three base model architectures that are widely used for clinical time series 42, 43 ; a long short-term memory network (LSTM), which is a baseline of mortality benchmarks 39, 44 , a gated recurrent unit (GRU), the second widely used recurrent variant for irregularly sampled clinical time series 45 and a transformer encoder 46 , which relates all hours of a stay to each other instead of reading them in sequence.
text.formatted: We compared three base model architectures that are widely used for clinical time series <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> ; a long short-term memory network (LSTM), which is a baseline of mortality benchmarks <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> , a gated recurrent unit (GRU), the second widely used recurrent variant for irregularly sampled clinical time series <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">45</ref> and a transformer encoder <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> , which relates all hours of a stay to each other instead of reading them in sequence.

text.text: Each architecture condenses the 48 hours into an internal representation of the patient, from which a final layer computes the predicted probability.
One of the uncertainty measures, the representation density, scores a patient by how close the patient's internal representation lies to those of the training cohort.
This assumes that patients who differ in their inputs also differ in the model's representations 36 .
text.formatted: This assumes that patients who differ in their inputs also differ in the model's representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36</ref> .

text.text: To explore whether enforcing this property has an impact on the results, we trained additional variants of the GRU and LSTM in which spectral normalization limits how strongly the network can stretch differences between patients in the representation space, and a residual block limits how strongly it can compress them 28, 35, 47 .

Models were trained with the Adam optimizer 48 and binary cross-entropy.

text.text: Hyperparameters, including the number of passes through the training data (epochs, 10 to 40), were selected per architecture with Optuna 49 via a validation split of the training pool (Supplementary Table 3, Supplementary Table 4, Supplementary Note 4); the constrained variants used those of their base architecture.

text.text: Each model was trained ten times with different random seeds, and the ten models of an architecture were also combined into a deep ensemble by averaging their predicted probabilities 50 .

text.text: Through Monte Carlo dropout, we obtain a predictive distribution for each patient using 30 dropout masks 51 .

text.text: The passes used the trained deterministic models themselves, with every dropout layer that was active in training also active at prediction time.
The dropout uncertainty measures were calculated from the 30 predicted mortality probabilities and their corresponding log-odds.
The equations for all components are given in Supplementary Note 1.
Each model returns an estimated probability that the patient dies in hospital.
A prediction was classified as positive if this probability exceeded 0.1288, the mortality rate of the training pool.
A prediction was therefore misclassified if the classification differed from the observed outcome.
A threshold of 0.5 was examined as a sensitivity analysis in Supplementary Note 2.
We compared three uncertainty measures, all computed per patient.
The first is the predictive entropy of a single model.
It is highest when the predicted probability is near 0.5 and zero when the model is certain:
The second comes from repeating a prediction either through T=30 Monte Carlo dropout passes or through the T=10 members of a deep ensemble.

With 𝑝 𝑖 (𝑡) being the prediction of pass or member 𝑡, the entropy of the averaged prediction is split into a part that the repeated predictions share and a part that reflects their disagreement 51, 52 : 𝑈 alea (𝑖)= 1 𝑇 ∑ 𝐻 𝑇 𝑡=1 (𝑝 𝑖 (𝑡) ).

text.text: (3) MI(𝑖)=𝑈 total (𝑖)-𝑈 alea (𝑖)≥0.
Total predictive uncertainty (𝑈 total ) is the entropy of the averaged mortality prediction.
The aleatoric component (𝑈 alea ) is the average entropy of the individual predictions and represents uncertainty within those predictions.
Their difference, mutual information (MI), measures disagreement between predictions and serves as the epistemic uncertainty measure.
MI is zero when all predictions agree, even if each prediction remains uncertain.
These definitions apply to both Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensembles.
For Monte Carlo dropout, we also calculated the logit variance, the variance of the log-odds across the 30 passes, as a second measure of epistemic uncertainty (Supplementary Note 1, Eq.
The third kind, representation density, is computed from a single forward pass of a single model.
Following deep deterministic uncertainty 28 , a Gaussian model with one component per outcome class is fitted to the internal representations ℎ of the training patients.
text.formatted: Following deep deterministic uncertainty <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28</ref> , a Gaussian model with one component per outcome class is fitted to the internal representations ℎ of the training patients.

text.text: We used the negative logarithm of the estimated density as the uncertainty score, with higher values indicating greater unfamiliarity: with class frequencies 𝜋 𝑐 , means 𝜇 𝑐 and covariances 𝛴 𝑐 ; high values of 𝑠(ℎ) indicate a patient unlike the training data.

Five further variants were evaluated on the same representations: a covariance shared across classes, a three-component mixture per class, the density on lengthnormalized representations 53 , a background-corrected relative density score, and the relative Mahalanobis distance of Ren et al. 26 (Supplementary Note 7).
text.formatted: Five further variants were evaluated on the same representations: a covariance shared across classes, a three-component mixture per class, the density on lengthnormalized representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> , a background-corrected relative density score, and the relative Mahalanobis distance of Ren et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26</ref> (Supplementary Note 7).

text.text: The density was also refitted on a class-balanced subset of the training pool as a sensitivity analysis.
Discrimination was measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and by the area under the precision-recall curve relative to the mortality rate (AUPRC lift).
The primary calibration measure was the calibration slope, estimated by a logistic regression of each patient's observed outcome on the model's log-odds, without grouping patients into bins 6, 54 .
text.formatted: The primary calibration measure was the calibration slope, estimated by a logistic regression of each patient's observed outcome on the model's log-odds, without grouping patients into bins <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54</ref> .

text.text: A slope of 1 is ideal; below 1, high predicted risks are too high and low predicted risks too low.
A linear fit on the deciles of Fig. 1 served as a sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Note 5).
text.formatted: A linear fit on the deciles of Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> served as a sensitivity analysis (Supplementary Note 5).

text.text: We also report the expected calibration error over deciles of the predicted risk (ECE; Supplementary Note 6) 55, 56 and the cross-entropy relative to a constant prediction of the mortality rate (skill; Supplementary Fig. 7).

text.text: Each uncertainty measure was evaluated at three levels, corresponding to each of the research questions:

Level 1, cohort separation, is the AUROC of the measure for distinguishing external from internal test patients: the probability that a randomly chosen external patient has the higher value, with 0.5 corresponding to chance and values above 0.5 to a measure that rises after transfer.
Level 2, error detection, is the AUROC of the measure for distinguishing misclassified from correctly classified external patients.

Errors were those of the prediction used together with the uncertainty measure: for single-model and Monte Carlo measures those of the model's own prediction without dropout, for ensemble measures those of the ensemble mean.
Level 3, selective prediction, asks whether deferring the most uncertain patients to clinical review reduces the errors among those who remain.

Patients were accepted from the most certain downward, and the misclassification rate among the k accepted patients, 𝑅(𝑘), was averaged over all 𝑘 to give the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) 57, 58 .
text.formatted: Patients were accepted from the most certain downward, and the misclassification rate among the k accepted patients, 𝑅(𝑘), was averaged over all 𝑘 to give the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">58</ref> .

text.text: Subtracting the area of an oracle that accepts all correctly classified patients first removes the effect of the overall error rate 59 :
text.formatted: Subtracting the area of an oracle that accepts all correctly classified patients first removes the effect of the overall error rate <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">59</ref> :

text.text: Lower values are better, and 0 is ideal.
We also report the misclassification rate among the accepted patients when the 20% most uncertain are deferred (risk at 80% coverage).
Patients with identical uncertainty measure values were accepted in the order of the cohort file, so that the result is reproducible (Supplementary Note 8).
Levels 2 and 3 were also computed on the internal test set as a baseline without distribution shift (Supplementary Table 12).
text.formatted: Levels 2 and 3 were also computed on the internal test set as a baseline without distribution shift (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">12</ref>).

text.text: Together, the three levels correspond to the two use cases examined in this study: Level 1 tests whether a measure warns of poorer overall performance after transfer, and Levels 2 and 3 whether it identifies the predictions that need review.
